own_scenes.desc: Nevermind de Nirvana (noviembre de 1991) llega al número uno el 11 de enero de 1992 y acaba con el reinado del lite metal. Los medios abrazan a Kurt Cobain y Eddie Vedder, las radios crean formatos «alternativos», la gran emisora de metal de Los Ángeles, KNAC, se vende en 1995 y MTV cancela Headbangers Ball en 1996; hasta Kerrang! se abre a la nueva moda, y los críticos, que crecieron con el rock universitario, ven por fin validado su gusto. El grunge no es metal aunque comparte la guitarra y la voz fuerte: alterna partes duras y suaves, canta el dolor y la desesperación, viste de tienda de segunda mano e identifica a la generación X con los débiles, frente al poder y el placer del metal («Somos pesados, pero no heavy metal», dice Krist Novoselic). Hacia 1998 el alternativo está moribundo.

refs.q: But Seattle-based Nirvana ended lite metal’s reign; its major-label debut, Nevermind, released in November of that year, climbed to the top of the chart on January 11, 1992.
refs.para: Cooler heads pinned metal’s demise on the rise of the Seattle-spawned style, grunge. Metal’s major market had mainly been in lite metal (what Was called hard rock in the 1970s). In 1991, lite metal had a banner year. With a massive fan base and the new SoundScan technology (making retail sales figures less biased by prejudice and wishful thinking), albums by Skid Row, Motley Crue, Van Halen, and Guns N’ Roses³ each debuted at number one on Billboard’s 1991 charts. But Seattle-based Nirvana ended lite metal’s reign; its major-label debut, Nevermind, released in November of that year, climbed to the top of the chart on January 11, 1992. A flock of other grunge bands followed in their wake.
refs.chapter: Cap. 8: El metal en los noventa

refs.q: “We’re heavy, but we’re not heavy metal,” Nirvana’s Chris Novoselic said.
refs.para: Grunge was not metal, but it shared metal’s guitar focus and strong lead singer. The styles had different song structures; grunge tended toward alternating hard and soft parts. Its hurt-and-despair lyrical focus didn’t particularly overlap with metal’s either. “We’re heavy, but we’re not heavy metal,” Nirvana’s Chris Novoselic said.⁵ “Yet another misunderstanding surrounding Nirvana,” a Rolling Stone writer opined, “is that the band plays, or even embraces, heavy metal—a myth perpetuated by reams of rave reviews from metal mags and an appearance on MTV’s Headbanger’s Ball. . . .”⁶ Novoselic emphasized the desire to distance grunge from that uncool genre: “Metal’s searching for an identity because it’s exhausted itself, so they’re going to latch onto us.”⁷

podcast.title: North American Term Origin (1980)
podcast.body: The term "alternative" in North America dates back to at least 1980, emerging as rock began to fragment. It originally described music from artists rejected by major labels due to smaller audiences, finding homes with small regional labels like Berserkli and Rounder. These labels and their music were seen as an "alternative" to the mainstream. "Now alternative dates back to at least 1980, a time when rock was really starting to fragment."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Times Square Soundtrack as Pioneer (1980)
podcast.body: The soundtrack for the 1980 movie *Time Square* was notable for being one of the very first to feature the nascent alternative music of the day, specifically punk rock and new wave. Despite its commercial failure, it offered an early glimpse into cutting-edge music for those who acquired it. "The soundtrack is notable in that it was one of the very first to feature the nascent alternative music of the day."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Growth and Diversity (1991-1995)
podcast.body: The period between 1991 and 1995 was described as a "wild ride" for alternative music, with new sounds, songs, and scenes emerging daily. This era encompassed grunge, American indie, the Lollapalooza generation, gangster rap, and the early stages of Britpop, showcasing immense musical diversity. "it was a wild ride between 91 and 95 was my favorite era of music because every day you come into work and there'd be this new sound, this new song, this new scene that we never heard of."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 1000th Episode of the Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Peak Era (1991-1995)
podcast.body: The period between 1991 and 1995 was considered the speaker's favorite era of music, as every day brought a new sound, song, or scene, indicating a rapid and exciting evolution of alternative music. "And it was, it was, it was a wild ride between 91 and 95 was my favorite era of music because every day you come into work and there'd be this new sound, this new song, this new scene that we never heard of."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: OGHONM 1000th Episode: The Q&A From the Live Recording

podcast.title: Underrepresentation in Pre-SoundScan Charts (Before May 25, 1991)
podcast.body: Under the old, unreliable sales reporting system, alternative music was one of two genres found to be significantly underrepresented. SoundScan's accurate data revealed its true commercial potential, leading to a subsequent explosion. "The first was country, and the second was alternative."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Singles Movie and Soundtrack (1992) as Golden Age Beginning
podcast.body: The movie *Singles* (1992) and its soundtrack appeared in a world where alternative and grunge music "ruled everywhere," solidifying a "golden age of alt rock-based soundtracks in the 1990s." The film, featuring contemporary music and cameos from grunge bands, significantly contributed to making the "grunge tent even bigger." "Now for me, this also ushered in a golden age of alt rock-based soundtracks in the 1990s."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Evolution (Since 1993)
podcast.body: Since February 1993, alternative music has undergone numerous changes and cycles, transitioning from the decline of the Manchester Sound to the rise of Grunge, Industrial, Punk comebacks, and then fragmentation and resurrections of other styles. "alternative music has gone through many changes in cycles."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: The Crow Soundtrack (1994) at Peak Alternative Period
podcast.body: *The Crow* soundtrack, released in 1994, was noted for being curated "right at the peak of a whole alternative in Lollapaloo's period." The music supervisors successfully captured the dark and fitting atmosphere of the film with contributions from bands like The Cure, Rage Against the Machine, and Stone Temple Pilots. "Again, this was 1994, right at the peak of a whole alternative in Lollapaloo's period, and the music supervisors nailed it."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Warped Tour's Initial Focus (1995)
podcast.body: The first Warped Tour in 1995 was designed as a "baby brother" to Lollapalooza, featuring a collection of up-and-coming alternative bands across two stages. "The first version was designed as kind of a baby brother to Lola, Paloza, a collection of up and coming alternative bands performing on two stages."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Warped Tour Content Pivot (1996)
podcast.body: After securing Vans as a title sponsor in 1996, the Warped Tour shifted its musical focus away from broad-range alternative to concentrate more specifically on punk and music associated with skate culture. "Kevin moved the festival from broad range alternative to focusing on punk and other music that went well with skate culture."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Resurgence (2004)
podcast.body: By late 2002 and definitively by 2004, Alt Rock experienced a resurgence with the emergence of many new and exciting bands. "By late 2002, there was a sense that maybe something was starting to bubble up from the underground again...By 2004, Alt Rock was back with all kinds of new exciting bands."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Unconventionality in 2008
podcast.body: In an early 2008 meeting at Island Records, executives debated whether a "banjo band" could be the "next big alternative band," indicating a need for fresh sounds in the genre amidst a challenging industry climate. "This is 2008. We need the next big alternative band."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: "Big Bang" Origin
podcast.body: Alternative music emerged as a "big bang" from the two core principles of 1970s punk rock: a musical reset and a DIY attitude. This led to chain reactions of new ideas, sounds, attitudes, fashion, belief systems, and general approaches, breaking rules and exploring new concepts. "Taken together, these two principles resulted in what can be described as the big bang for what would later be called alternative music."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Post-Punk Explosion Part 7: All the rest

podcast.title: "College Rock" as Predecessor
podcast.body: For a period during the 1980s and 1990s, non-mainstream rock was sometimes referred to as "college rock," largely because it was the type of music frequently broadcast on campus radio stations. However, this term was considered somewhat limiting, especially for non-college audiences, leading to the eventual adoption of more inclusive terms like "alternative" and "Indie." "For a while, some called it college rock because it seemed to be the kind of music that you heard on campus radio stations."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: "Dookie" Grammy Award
podcast.body: Grimbey's album "Dookie" was recognized for its excellence in the genre, receiving the Grammy Award for Best Alternative Music Album. This award solidified its status and influence within the alternative music landscape of the 1990s. "También te hubo el Grammy al mejor álbum de música alternativa."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: Green Day - Dookie (¿el concierto más divertido de los '90?)

podcast.title: 1990s Keyboard Dominance
podcast.body: In the early 1990s, before the massive success of "Smells Like Teen Spirit," alternative rock radio was largely dominated by keyboard-based music from bands like Depeche Mode, INXS, New Order, and The Cure, with a generally "left-leaning" sound. "alt rock radio at the time was about Depeche Mode and in excess, New Order, The Curie Ratio and Left Leaning Alternative Music that was more often than not keyboard based."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: 90s Revolution
podcast.body: The early 1990s witnessed an "alternative revolution" in music, characterized by an abundance of new and cool sounds led by Grunge, marking a special time where new songs, artists, sounds, and scenes emerged daily. "It's led by Grunge, but supported by all manner of alternative music."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Post-Punk Explosion Part 1: New Wave

podcast.title: Adrift Period (Early 2000s)
podcast.body: At the start of the new century, after the decline of Electronica and Nu Metal, the Alt Rock scene was largely "adrift," with many bands sounding similar and few new stars emerging, apart from occasional "indie brilliance." "for a while, the whole alt-roxying was, well, let's be honest, pretty adrift. Outside the occasional burst of indie brilliance...things all really did sound the same for a few years and no real stars emerged."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Alternative to Mainstream
podcast.body: The term "alternative" arose because signing to independent labels provided an alternative to the mainstream music industry for radical new music like punk. These labels and the music they promoted became known as "alternative." "Signing to these independent labels was an alternative to the mainstream. They became known as alternative labels, and the music they promoted was alternative music."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Indie Rock: Part 1

podcast.title: Basic Enduring Sound
podcast.body: Alternative music is listed as one of the basic and enduring sounds that will never go away, but is continuously challenged by new genres. "The basic sounds are still with us. Rock, alternative, indie, Goth, industrial, metal, synth-based music, ska, reggae, and so on. They're never going to go away."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of the 2010s Part 3: The New Genres

podcast.title: Birth of the "Alternative Nation"
podcast.body: The proliferation and acceptance of this music in the 1990s led to the coining of the term "alternative nation," signifying the widespread cultural impact of this genre. "It was the birth of what we call in the 90s the alternative nation."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Björk's Debut Album as Collector's Item
podcast.body: Björk's 1977 debut album became a "holy grail" for collectors in independent and alternative music. "este disco se ha convertido uno de los santos griales del coleccionismo de la música independiente y alternativa."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan

podcast.title: British "Indie" vs. American "Alternative"
podcast.body: In Britain, the term "alternative" did not gain widespread traction; instead, "indie" served as the preferred word for this type of music, reflecting a different linguistic and cultural adoption of similar musical phenomena. "In Britain, the A word alternative never really cut out. Instead the word indie was their word for alternative."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Post-Punk Explosion Part 7: All the rest

podcast.title: Campus Radio's Role in Popularization
podcast.body: Campus radio stations played a critical role in the growth and networking of the alternative scene. They specialized in playing music from independent labels and, as they became more influential and connected through magazines and conventions, they began consistently referring to this music as "alternative." "Campus stations specialized in this stuff."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Catch-All Umbrella Term
podcast.body: Similar to New Wave, "alternative" functioned as a broad umbrella term encompassing all music that emerged following punk and consciously rejected mainstream commercialization. It covered a vast stylistic spectrum, from low-fi fuzzy guitar rock (Sonic Youth) to electronic pop (Depeche Mode), heavy industrial music (Skinny Puppy, Ministry), and even delicate music from major-label artists (Kate Bush, Tori Amos). "Like New Wave, this was a catch-all umbrella term that described all the music that came in the wake of punk."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Challenges in Discovery Today
podcast.body: While good alternative music still exists, the sheer volume of available music makes it much harder to discover new artists that create the same level of excitement experienced in earlier days. "So it's the good music is there. It's just there's so much of it. It takes a lot longer to find stuff that's going to make you excited like you were back in the day."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: OGHONM 1000th Episode: The Q&A From the Live Recording

podcast.title: Contemporary Meaning
podcast.body: Today, "alternative music" continues to exist, often referred to as "indie" or "underground music." It describes cutting-edge rock that operates below the mainstream radar, found in small clubs and niche record stores, and is typically sought out by a more selective audience. "So alternative music, rock that is an alternative to everything we see in here in the mainstreams till exists, is just that you have to look for it and maybe sometime call it Indie or underground music."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Crossover with Indie
podcast.body: There is significant crossover between the terms "Indie" and "alternative," though it eventually became possible for an "alternative" act to sign with a major label. "But bottom line here is that there's plenty of crossover between the terms Indy and alternative, although it later became possible to be an alternative act on a major label, but we'll get to that."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Indie Rock: Part 1

podcast.title: Cycles of Sounds and Trends
podcast.body: Alternative music, having existed for over 45 years, has seen its sounds and trends cycle through multiple times. This occurs as new generations discover and adopt musical styles that appeal to them, leading to periodic revivals. "Alternative music has been around long enough, 45 years in counting, that certain sounds and trends have cycled through maybe a couple of times, as new generations pick up the ball and run with whatever music they seem to like."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Defining Attitude of the 1980s
podcast.body: In the late 1980s, the term "Alternative" began to describe a certain attitude in rock music, encompassing anything that couldn't fit into regular categories, characterized by being new, weird, and hated by the mainstream. "If you couldn't categorize a song or an artist by tossing it into any of the regular buckets, then there was only one other bucket you could use, and it quickly filled up."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Definition in the 1950s
podcast.body: In the 1950s, if rock and roll was considered the alternative to the mainstream, then its early stars, such as Elvis Presley, could be viewed as the first alternative music stars. "if rocket roll was the alternative to the mainstream in the 1950s, we could also say that Elvis was our first alternative music star too."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Dependence on Pioneers
podcast.body: Without performers like Iggy Pop, today's New Rock and Alternative Music "wouldn't be possible," emphasizing the foundational role of early icons in shaping contemporary genres. "We need to care because without these performers, today's New Rock and Alternative Music wouldn't be possible."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What's The Big Deal About Iggy Pop

podcast.title: Distinct from Mainstream
podcast.body: Regardless of its precise origin, the music labeled "alternative" was fundamentally seen as an alternative to the mainstream. It represented sounds and artists that were not part of the commercial establishment. "And yes, this music was an alternative to the mainstream."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Dominant Force (Mid-90s)
podcast.body: By the mid-1990s, Alternative Music and Modern Rock were described as the "dominant musical force in the universe." "Alternative music and Modern Rock was the dominant musical force in the universe."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Dominant Radio Format (Early 1990s)
podcast.body: In January 1993, observing the rise of grunge and Lollapalooza, new radio station management decided to commit fully to an alternative format, rather than adopting country music. This strategic move aimed to cater to new listeners drawn to the burgeoning alternative scene. "the new boss has doubled down on an alternative format."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 1000th Episode of the Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Driving Factor in 1990s Growth
podcast.body: The rise of the alternative scene in the 1990s, taking over from older mainstream bands, was a key factor working in favor of Canadian rock. This shift in musical tastes created an opportune environment for new Canadian artists to flourish. "and the sea change in music, with the alternative scene taking over from older mainstream bands."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Roots of the 90s CanRock Explosion

podcast.title: Early 1990s Popularity Boom
podcast.body: The early 1990s saw a significant surge in the popularity of alternative music and punk, marked by the widespread success of bands such as Nirvana, Pearl Jam, and The Smashing Pumpkins. This era fueled considerable interest among major record labels in acquiring California punk bands. "With alternative music and punk getting really, really hot, you got to remember this is when Nirvana and Pearl Jam and the smashing pumpkins were blowing up everywhere."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Green Day: From their Beginning to 2005

podcast.title: Early Lollapalooza Focus
podcast.body: Lollapalooza was described as the touring music festival for the "alternative generation" for a few years after its 1992 expansion. "And for the next couple of years, Lala Palusa was the touring music festival for the alternative generation."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Emergence as Umbrella Term
podcast.body: The term "alternative" became the preferred word among fans and critics to describe a new wave of music that diverged from the mainstream. This term gained prominence as collective sales of these distinct bands grew into millions of records and concert tickets annually. "The word that fans and critics gravitated to was alternative."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Emphasis on Authenticity
podcast.body: In the early 90s, as Weezer developed their sound, there was an increasing emphasis on authenticity in the alternative music scene. This led Rivers Cuomo to worry that his past as a metalhead could be detrimental to the group's perception and chances. "The more alternative sounding Weezer got, the more emphasis was placed on authenticity."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Rivers Cuomo and Weezer - Alt-Rock's Nerd Heroes Part 1

podcast.title: Evolution of Mainstream Status
podcast.body: Alternative music experienced a trajectory from being a niche genre to becoming mainstream, but in the current era of ubiquitous streaming, it has reverted to a more niche status within the vast "monopoly of music." "Alternative music has become again a nichey, more of a niche thing than it used to be. It was niche that it became the mainstream. And then now it's just part of this giant monopoly of music that everybody can listen to for free."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: OGHONM 1000th Episode: The Q&A From the Live Recording

podcast.title: Faith No More's 90s Success
podcast.body: Faith No More, with Mike Patton as singer, achieved early widespread success in the alternative scene of the 1990s. "And within a year, Faith No More was all over the video channels, and we're on their way to becoming one of the biggest early successes of the alternative 90s."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Groups That Changed Their Front-Person and Survived

podcast.title: First True Alternative Band – The Velvet Underground
podcast.body: The Velvet Underground is widely regarded by many as the first true alternative band. Their innovative sound and unconventional approach, including Maureen Tucker's unique drumming style, set them apart and influenced subsequent alternative music movements. "our group considered by many to be the first true alternative band."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Foundational Band
podcast.body: The Velvet Underground is frequently identified as the first alternative band, largely due to their signature rough, raw sound which was heavily imbued with distortion, feedback, and noise. Their experimental approach set a precedent for later alternative music. "Louis previous band, the Velvet Underground, has often been called the first alternative band."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Distortion and Feedback

podcast.title: Fragmentation and Loss of Meaning (1980s-1990s)
podcast.body: As the 1980s transitioned into the 1990s, alternative music fragmented into numerous subgenres, including various forms of punk, hardcore punk, synthesizer-based music, goth, and industrial. This proliferation made the term increasingly confusing, especially after the mainstream success of Nirvana and grunge effectively made the "alternative world mainstream," causing the word to lose its original intent of signifying an *alternative* to established norms. "As the 80s turned into the 90s, alternative music began to fragment, into dozens and dozens of different streams."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Genre Classification Example
podcast.body: "Alternative" is used to describe the genre of Queens of the Stone Age's song "The Way You Used To Do," released in 2017. "It's labeled as an alternative song released in 2017..."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Historical Ostracization of Non-Alternative Music Fans
podcast.body: In 1996, working at an alternative radio station meant that admitting a liking for non-alternative music (such as Led Zeppelin) could lead to severe professional and social repercussions, including ostracization, firing, and physical assault. "So if you were in 1996, said, you know what? I kind of like Led Zeppler, who'd you just prized? You would be completely ostracized, probably fired and beaten up on the way out."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: OGHONM 1000th Episode: The Q&A From the Live Recording

podcast.title: Impact on INXS Sales
podcast.body: The public's growing fascination with alternative music, along with grunge, contributed to the underperformance of INXS albums like *Welcome to Wherever You Are* (1992) and *Full Moon, Dirty Hearts* (1993). "A victim of the public's growing fascination with grunge and all things alternative."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: John Hughes Films' Impact (1980s)
podcast.body: John Hughes' 1980s movies, such as *Sixteen Candles*, *The Breakfast Club*, and *Pretty in Pink*, featured carefully curated soundtracks heavily mined from the alternative rock of the day. These films were instrumental in introducing millions of people to bands like New Order, The Smiths, and The Jesus and Mary Chain, significantly expanding the genre's audience in North America, especially for British acts. "Each one of these movies was accompanied by a carefully curated soundtrack that was heavily mined from the alt rock of the day."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Lack of Historical Documentation (Early 1990s)
podcast.body: In late 1992, there was almost no existing historical writing on alternative music, with sources limited to old magazine articles, record company materials, and year-end charts. "At the time there was almost zero historical writing on alternative music. The only sources were articles in old magazines and boxes of stuff dropped off by record companies and some year-end best of charts."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Layne Staley's Vocal Appeal
podcast.body: Layne Staley's distinct vocal style garnered appeal from both alternative kids and metal fans. "And those vocals appealed to both metal fans and alternative kids."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Groups That Changed Their Front-Person and Survived

podcast.title: Lineage Outside Mainstream Rock
podcast.body: The word "alternative" eventually became a broad umbrella term for rock music that was distinct from the lineage of bands like The Beatles, The Rolling Stones, and Led Zeppelin. Instead, its roots were traced to artists such as David Bowie, Iggy Pop, The Velvet Underground, and The Ramones. "the word alternative became more widely used as this umbrella term for rock music that was different that did not descend from the Beatles and the Stones and Led Zeppelin, but from Bowie and Iggy Pop and the Velvet Underground and the Ramones."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Lollapalooza's Original Focus (1990s)
podcast.body: In its original conception in 1990, Lollapalooza was a touring festival that showcased "left-of-center and alternative bands," solidifying its place as a crucial element of 1990s music culture. "When La La Palosa was first conceived in 1990, it was a full-blown touring festival of Weirdos, featuring the best in left-of-center and alternative bands."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 100 Greatest Rock Moments of the Millennium So Far - Part 4: (70-61)

podcast.title: Lollapalooza's Role
podcast.body: The Lollapalooza Festival served as the "premier live event" for propagating the "gospel" of the alternative nation for much of the 1990s, indicating its crucial role in the genre's development and reach.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 9

podcast.title: Meaning by Grunge Era (Early 90s)
podcast.body: By the early 1990s and the grunge era, "alternative" described a new generation of music descended from punk and new wave, rather than from bands like Led Zeppelin or The Beatles. It signified an aesthetic and sensibility, not merely a record label origin, and largely lost its countercultural significance. "by the time we got to the grunge era of the early 90s, alternative was being used to describe a new generation of music that had descended from punk and new wave and not from Led Zeppelin and the Beatles."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Modern Usage and Diminished Relevance
podcast.body: While some "artsy types" favored "post-modern" (which was sometimes simplified to "modern rock"), the most common phrase for contemporary rock music is now simply "New Rock." Consequently, the word "alternative" has largely lost its original meaning and intended purpose, as what was once considered alternative frequently now occupies the mainstream. "So as a result, the word alternative has lost its meaning, or at least the intent of its original meaning."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Murky Etymology of "Alternative Music"
podcast.body: The precise origin and etymology of the phrase "alternative music" are considered uncertain or "murky." Several theories exist regarding how the term came to be widely adopted. "Well, the etymology of the phrase alternative music is murky, but let's try."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Nebulous Umbrella Term of the 1990s
podcast.body: "Alternative" emerged in the early 1990s as a "nebulous umbrella term" used to classify bands that were so unique they "defied description." It came to broadly signify "difference" and served as a category for artists like Tool, Red Hot Chili Peppers, Beastie Boys, and Rage Against the Machine, causing confusion due to its broadness. "Alternative came to mean difference. It was a basket in which to put bands that defied description."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Non-Mainstream Counterpart to Major Labels
podcast.body: For many years, rock music was bifurcated into the mainstream, populated by famous bands on major labels (e.g., Led Zeppelin, The Stones, The Beatles, ACDC, Van Halen), and a category of "all the music that didn't get mainstream attention." This latter category comprised music deemed too weird, different, or innovative for general media and the public, though it cultivated dedicated fan bases often experienced in smaller club settings rather than stadiums. "On the other side of this equation, there was all the music that didn't get mainstream attention. This was the stuff that was just too weird or too different or too innovative for the general media and the general public."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Origin of the Term
podcast.body: In the 1970s and early 1980s, "alternative music" became the term for music created by "weird kids" that was not played on mainstream radio or signed by major labels. Small independent record labels, offering a "career alternative" for these bands, became known as "alternative record companies," thereby defining the bands and their music as "alternative." "By the very early 1980s, those small indie labels had become known as alternative record companies because they provided a career option, a career alternative for the weird band who couldn't find homes with the majors."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Origin on Independent Labels (Late 1970s/Early 1980s)
podcast.body: The "alternative" designation originated with small, independent, niche record companies such as Epitaph, SST, Beserkley, Rounder, and Sire, which emerged in the late 1970s and early 1980s. These "alternative labels" were unaffiliated with major multinational corporations and provided a vital platform for groups influenced by the punk movement, often signing bands that major labels overlooked due to perceived lack of mass commercial appeal. "The only way these acts could get their music out there was to create alliances with small, independent, niche record companies who weren't affiliated with a major label."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Overtaking the Mainstream (Mid-90s)
podcast.body: The "grunge explosion" of the early to mid-1990s saw alternative rock transition from an underground form to the mainstream, largely replacing traditional mainstream rock acts. This shift made the term "alternative" somewhat contradictory, as it was no longer an alternative to anything, prompting a search for new terminology like "New Rock." "In other words, by the middle of the 90s, alternative music wasn't an alternative to anything anymore. It was now the mainstream, which caused much soul searching and hand-winging amongst musicians and fans like."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Post-Grunge Mainstream Shift
podcast.body: After the rise of grunge, alternative music, largely thanks to Nirvana's "Nevermind," eventually became mainstream music, losing its "alternative" status as it grew too big too fast, with guitar-bass-drums bands dominating. "It wasn't long before alt rock was no longer an alternative to anything."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Pre-Grunge Definition
podcast.body: Up until the 1990s, "Alternative" was an umbrella term for a wide variety of sounds that were "left of center," "weird to the mainstream music fan," and "ignored by the media." It included singer-songwriters, indie pop, industrial bands, synth groups, goth groups, noisy guitar bands, and even rap in the 80s. "There wasn't what anyone could call a defining sound."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Red Hot Chili Peppers' Rise to Prominence
podcast.body: The Red Hot Chili Peppers, with their album "Blood Sugar Sex Magik," transitioned from a mid-level band to one of the biggest groups of the alternative era. This shift was largely attributed to John Frusciante's vital contributions to the record. "took the chili peppers from, well, let's face it, a very good mid-level band to one of the biggest groups of that alternative era."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Long Strange Trip of John Frusciante Part 1

podcast.title: Relationship with "Indie"
podcast.body: The term "alternative" eventually became synonymous with "Indie," the British equivalent for independent labels and the music they produced (e.g., Mute, Factory, Rough Trade, Creation). Over time, "Indie" gained broader acceptance and ultimately superseded "alternative" as the preferred descriptor across the Atlantic, being perceived as "a better word." "The British had their alternative labels too, but they didn't call them that. They refer to their version as Indy as an independent."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Rise in Early 90s
podcast.body: In the early 1990s, Alternative Music was rising, leading to Iggy Pop being recognized once again as a legendary alt-rock pioneer, alongside other influential acts like The Velvet Underground and The Sex Pistols. "The early 90s were pretty good to Iggy. He was cleaned up and sounding better than he had in years, and at the same time, Indy and Alternative Music was rising up, and Iggy was once again named as a legendary alt-rock pioneer."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What's The Big Deal About Iggy Pop

podcast.title: Rise of the Term
podcast.body: The term "alternative music" arose as a categorization for artists who sounded different and recorded for smaller independent labels, providing an "alternative to whatever the mainstream was offering at the time." This followed the evolution from "college rock" to "indie groups." "hence the rise of the term alternative music."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Sexual Encounters Playlists Ranking
podcast.body: Alternative music was ranked as the fifth most common genre on playlists created to soundtrack sexual encounters, behind pop, hip hop, R&B, and Indy Rock, and ahead of EDM. "alternative was fifth."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Smashing Pumpkins' Significance (1990s)
podcast.body: The Smashing Pumpkins were described as one of the most important, influential, and bestselling bands of the "alternative nation" throughout the 1990s.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 9

podcast.title: Supplanted "College Rock"
podcast.body: The term "alternative" eventually replaced "college rock," which was used to describe music popular on campus radio stations. "This word alternative eventually supplanted the term college rock, which was being used to describe the music that found favor with campus radio stations."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: The Velvet Underground as Pioneers
podcast.body: The Velvet Underground is recognized as "probably the first ever alternative band" during their formative period in the 1960s. "They were probably the first ever alternative band when they were together for the first time around in the 1960s."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Theory 1: 1970s FM Radio
podcast.body: One theory suggests that "alternative" initially described certain FM radio stations in the 1970s. These stations would play music that was "slightly different" from the corporate rock staples like Styx, Journey, and Boston, occasionally integrating punk or New Wave tracks, thus offering an "alternative" programming choice. "Some say it originally described certain forms of FM radio in the 1970s, the kind of stations that would play slightly different music than all the rest."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Theory 2: Independent Record Labels
podcast.body: Another theory posits that the term originated from independent record labels. Bands whose sound was considered too "weird" or "radical" to secure deals with major labels had "no alternative" but to sign with smaller independent companies like SST, Epitaph, Berserkeley, Rounder, IRS, or Alternative Tentacles. Consequently, music recorded for these "alternative labels" became known as "alternative rock." "Another theory involves independent record labels."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Top Boinking Song for Playlists
podcast.body: An unnamed "alt rock song" was identified as topping the rock and alternative list for favorite "boinking" songs and consistently finished very high as the top alt rock song on playlists designed to soundtrack action in the bedroom. "This track topped the rock and alternative list for favorite boinking song."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Transformation in the 80s and 90s
podcast.body: New Order, formed by the remaining members of Joy Division, played a crucial role in transforming alternative music throughout the 1980s and into the 1990s, building upon the foundations laid by their previous band. "And of course, there's the work of New Order, who helped transform alternative music in the 80s and into the 90s."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What's the Big Deal About Joy Division?

podcast.title: UK Interchangeability with Indie
podcast.body: In the UK, the term "Indie" is often roughly interchangeable with "alternative." This is attributed to the specific structure of the British music industry, which provides independent artists a greater opportunity to penetrate the mainstream compared to North America. "In the UK, Indie can be roughly interchangeable with alternative."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Video-Driven Growth
podcast.body: Alternative music thrived through music videos. The visual medium provided a powerful platform for genres like grunge and alternative to gain widespread exposure and grow into significant cultural forces, influencing fashion, makeup, and sexuality among youth. "People learned about different types of music, grunge and alternative thrived, hip hop and rap grew into monsters."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
